overview:
In Jain traditions, architecture is not merely a technical craft but a material expression of cosmology, ethics, and the path to liberation. From the earliest narrative descriptions of the samavasarana—the divine preaching assembly of a Tirthankara—to the highly developed temple complexes of medieval Gujarat, Rajasthan, Karnataka, and beyond, built space is used to model an ordered, non-violent universe in which all beings can orient themselves toward moksha. Jain architecture therefore spans both imagined sacred structures described in scripture and the stone, brick, and metal constructions produced by communities over many centuries.

Scriptural accounts of the samavasarana provide one of the earliest and most detailed Jain "architectural" blueprints. The preaching hall is described as a vast, circular, tiered pavilion constructed by celestial beings immediately after a Tirthankara attains kevala-jñāna. Its concentric arrangement of halls for ascetics, laypeople, devas, animals, and other beings, together with four cardinal gateways and a central throne beneath a sacred tree, encodes Jain ideas of equality, non-hierarchy, and universal accessibility of dharma. The Tirthankara’s divyadhvani (divine sound) is said to be heard by all in their own language, reinforcing the notion that the architecture of the samavasarana is a spatial metaphor for non-violence and inclusivity rather than a mere spectacle.

Historical Jain temples and pilgrimage sites translate these cosmological and ethical ideas into durable materials. Early structures likely drew on pan-Indian forms such as stupas and rock-cut caves, but by the medieval period, distinct Jain temple idioms emerged, especially in western India. Complexes like Dilwara at Mount Abu, Śatruñjaya at Palitana, and Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa in Karnataka exhibit intricate mandapa (hall) systems, richly carved ceilings, and axial processional routes that guide the devotee from outer, more worldly spaces toward inner sanctums housing Jina images or, in some traditions, more abstract symbols. The use of mandalas and cosmological diagrams in planning—often related to the Vāstu Purusha Mandala and Jain cosmological charts—links the ground plan of the temple to the three worlds (loka) and the vertical ascent toward the siddha-śilā, the realm of liberated beings.

Different Jain sects and regional lineages have developed characteristic architectural preferences. Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka communities emphasize image worship and therefore build garbhagṛhas (sanctums) with seated or standing Jina icons, surrounded by circumambulatory paths and subsidiary shrines. Digambara temples often feature nude Jina images and may highlight monumental monolithic statues, as at Gommaṭeśvara in Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, while also maintaining smaller shrines and bhattārakas’ seats. Sthānakavāsī and some Terāpanthī groups historically favored image-less spaces, using simple halls for congregational worship and scriptural recitation, which reflects a different architectural response to the same doctrinal emphasis on internal purity and non-attachment. Across these variations, however, the orientation of buildings, the hierarchy of spaces, and the placement of images or seats for scripture recitation consistently aim to support right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct.

Jain architecture also functions as a social and educational institution. Temples and upāśrayas (monastic residences or community halls) serve as centers for teaching, manuscript preservation, and ritual practice. Their design often accommodates lecture halls, libraries, and spaces for collective fasting, confession (pratikramaṇa), and festival observances such as Paryuṣaṇa. In many regions, temple towers and shikharas historically acted as landmarks and wayfinding devices, signaling a place of refuge and ethical discipline. Modern Jain complexes sometimes consciously evoke the samavasarana in their circular or tiered layouts, using contemporary materials while retaining the symbolic emphasis on openness and equal access.

From a technical perspective, Jain architects and patrons have engaged with broader South Asian building sciences, including vāstu-śāstra, while interpreting them through Jain ethical lenses. Choices of materials, decorative programs, and structural innovations are often constrained by ahiṃsā: for example, care in avoiding harm to living beings during construction, and the use of iconography that emphasizes non-violence, restraint, and the multiplicity of viewpoints (anekāntavāda). Ceiling carvings, pillar designs, and narrative friezes frequently depict Tirthankara lives, samavasarana scenes, and cosmological diagrams, turning the building itself into a three-dimensional scripture. In this way, Jain architecture becomes both a physical shelter and a pedagogical environment, guiding the practitioner through space as a form of contemplative practice.

Contemporary Jain communities continue to experiment with architectural forms, from urban temples embedded in dense cityscapes to large pilgrimage campuses and convention centers inspired by samavasarana imagery. These projects raise ongoing questions about sustainability, accessibility, and the balance between grandeur and non-attachment. Yet the underlying impulse remains consistent with classical descriptions: to create spaces that mirror an ordered, non-violent cosmos and invite all beings—regardless of status or species—to encounter the teachings of the Jinas. Architecture, in this Jain sense, is a disciplined art of shaping space so that it supports ethical transformation and the gradual shedding of karma.

primary_sources.title: Aupapātika-sūtra (Samavasaraṇa section)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous Śvetāmbara canonical redactors
primary_sources.original_text: Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit passage describing the samavasaraṇa as the preaching assembly following kevala-jñāna, preserved in the Aupapātika-sūtra’s section traditionally titled "samavasaraṇa".
primary_sources.transliteration: samavasaraṇaṃ jina-kevalañāṇa-paccakkhaṃ savva-jīva-hita-kāraṇaṃ vibhāvitam ti (paraphrastic representation of the canonical description, not a critical-edition line).
primary_sources.translation: “The samavasaraṇa is the assembly made manifest after the Jina’s omniscience, for the benefit of all living beings.” (Paraphrased sense based on the Aupapātika-sūtra’s account of the preaching event and its universal audience.)
primary_sources.notes: This early Śvetāmbara canonical text focuses on the event of preaching rather than a fully developed architectural description. Later exegetical literature expands the spatial and structural details of the samavasaraṇa, but the Aupapātika-sūtra establishes its role as a sacred space where the Jina’s divyadhvani is heard by all beings in their own language.

primary_sources.title: Avasyaka-niryukti (Samavasaraṇa tract)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu; composed by early Śvetāmbara exegetes
primary_sources.original_text: Prakrit verses forming a tract of approximately 52 ślokas that describe the samavasaraṇa’s concentric halls, central caitya-vṛkṣa, throne, and the ordered seating of ascetics, devas, humans, and animals.
primary_sources.translation: “In the middle, upon the lion throne beneath the sacred tree, the Jina, omniscient and supreme in all the world, sits. Around him are many circles, known as the samavasaraṇa.” (Paraphrased sense capturing the spatial arrangement and centrality of the Jina in the tract.)
primary_sources.notes: The Avasyaka-niryukti integrates the samavasaraṇa description into a broader ‘Universal History’ and liturgical context. Modern scholarship identifies this tract as a key archetype for later Śvetāmbara accounts of the samavasaraṇa’s architecture, emphasizing its circular layout, tiered halls, and symbolic ordering of beings.

primary_sources.title: Bṛhatkalpa-bhāṣya (Samavasaraṇa excursus)
primary_sources.author: Attributed to Saṅghadāsa Gaṇi and later Śvetāmbara commentators
primary_sources.original_text: Prakrit and mixed Prakrit-Sanskrit commentary passages that unexpectedly introduce a detailed excursus on the samavasaraṇa, including measurements, tiers, and ritual aspects of the sacred space.
primary_sources.transliteration: samavasaraṇaṃ nāma mahā-maṇḍapaḥ, tatra trīṇi maṇḍalāni, madhye jina-āsanam, catur-diśaṃ dvāra-yuktam iti (paraphrastic summary in Sanskritized form).
primary_sources.translation: “The samavasaraṇa is a great pavilion: within it are three circles, in the middle the Jina’s seat, and it is furnished with gateways in the four directions.” (Paraphrased sense reflecting the bhāṣya’s architectural emphasis.)
primary_sources.notes: In the Bṛhatkalpa-bhāṣya, the samavasaraṇa appears as a pseudo-exegetical excursus, suggesting that its description had become a recognized doctrinal and ritual topic. The text elaborates on spatial organization, ritual movement, and the symbolic meaning of the structure, contributing significantly to later temple representations of the samavasaraṇa.

primary_sources.title: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra (Lives of the 63 Illustrious Persons)
primary_sources.author: Hemacandra
primary_sources.original_text: Classical Sanskrit narrative passages describing the construction of the samavasaraṇa by devas after a Tirthankara’s enlightenment, including references to jeweled pavilions, banners, and the ordered seating of beings.
primary_sources.transliteration: kevala-jñānam avāpya jinaḥ, tataḥ samavasaraṇaṃ divyaṃ devaiḥ kāritaṃ, ratna-stambha-śobhitaṃ, catur-diśa-dvāra-yuktaṃ, sarva-bhūta-samāgama-sthānam iti (paraphrastic summary).
primary_sources.translation: “Having attained omniscience, the Jina then had a divine samavasaraṇa constructed by the gods, adorned with jewel-pillars, furnished with gateways in the four directions, and serving as the place where all beings assemble.” (Paraphrased sense based on Hemacandra’s narrative style.)
primary_sources.notes: Hemacandra’s work systematizes Jain universal history and provides richly literary accounts of key events, including the samavasaraṇa. His descriptions influenced later visual and architectural representations, especially in western India, where temple reliefs and silver models depict samavasaraṇa scenes with circular tiers and central Jina images.

primary_sources.title: Tiloyapaṇṇatti and related cosmological texts
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Yativṛṣabha (Digambara)
primary_sources.original_text: Jain Prakrit cosmological descriptions of the three worlds (triloka), the shape of the universe, and the location of realms such as the siddha-śilā, which later inform temple planning and cosmological diagrams.
primary_sources.transliteration: lokaṃ tiṇṇaṃ bhāgaṃ vadanti—ūrdhva-lokaṃ, madhya-lokaṃ, adho-lokaṃ; tattha siddha-śilā upari, jīvaṇa-saṃsāra-majjhe maṇḍalā bahū (paraphrastic summary).
primary_sources.translation: “They speak of the world as having three parts—upper world, middle world, and lower world; there, above, is the siddha-śilā, and in the midst of the wandering of living beings are many circles.” (Paraphrased sense capturing the cosmological framework.)
primary_sources.notes: Although not an architectural manual, the Tiloyapaṇṇatti and related cosmological texts provide the conceptual background for Jain mandalas, temple diagrams, and vertical symbolism. Temple architects and patrons have drawn on these cosmological models to align ground plans, vertical axes, and decorative programs with the Jain understanding of the universe.

misconceptions.myth: Jain architecture is purely decorative and focuses only on intricate stone carving without deeper meaning.
misconceptions.reality: While Jain temples are renowned for their fine carving and ornamentation, their layouts, vertical organization, and iconographic programs are grounded in Jain cosmology and ethics. Structures such as the samavasaraṇa, mandapas, and shikharas are designed to embody non-violence, equality of beings, and the ascent toward liberation, turning the building into a three-dimensional map of the path to moksha rather than a merely aesthetic object.

misconceptions.myth: All Jain temples follow a single, uniform architectural style centered on image worship.
misconceptions.reality: Jain architecture varies significantly across sects and regions. Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka and many Digambara communities build image-centered temples, but Sthānakavāsī and some Terāpanthī groups historically favored image-less halls for congregational worship. Regional idioms in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Karnataka, and elsewhere also produce distinct forms. Despite these differences, the underlying aim of supporting ethical practice and contemplation remains shared.

misconceptions.myth: The samavasaraṇa is simply a mythological structure with no relevance to actual Jain buildings.
misconceptions.reality: Although the samavasaraṇa is described as a divine, celestial assembly hall, its spatial logic and symbolism have strongly influenced Jain temple architecture and ritual spaces. Circular or tiered models of the samavasaraṇa are commonly found in temples as silver or stone structures, and modern complexes sometimes adopt samavasaraṇa-inspired layouts. The concept thus serves as a bridge between scriptural imagination and built environments.

misconceptions.myth: Jain architecture is detached from broader South Asian building sciences and exists in isolation.
misconceptions.reality: Jain architects and patrons have engaged with wider South Asian traditions of vāstu-śāstra and mandala planning, adapting them to Jain doctrinal priorities. Temple ground plans, orientations, and structural systems often follow shared regional norms, but they are interpreted through Jain values such as ahiṃsā, aparigraha, and anekāntavāda, resulting in buildings that participate in broader architectural cultures while maintaining distinct religious meanings.
